definition: Psychological field here means the sphere or domain of mental life and psychological processes, as distinct from bodily or neurological events. It refers broadly to matters studied by psychology, such as thought, attention, memory, and will.

reasons: The packet only supports the phrase "purely psychological field" in a general historical sense; it does not define the term as a distinct "sphere or domain of mental life" contrasted with bodily or neurological events.

The examples in the packet are limited to topics James says will be treated in later chapters (instinct, stream of thought, attention, discrimination, association, memory, aesthetics, will); the definition adds a broader modern gloss about what psychology studies that is not explicitly stated here.
The definition presents a concept-style gloss rather than a source-grounded historical definition, and it goes beyond the supplied passage's wording.

The packet does not support the claim that “psychological field” means “the sphere or domain of mental life and psychological processes, as distinct from bodily or neurological events.” It only contains the phrase “purely psychological field,” without defining it that way.

The packet does not explicitly define “psychological field” as “matters studied by psychology” or as a broad domain encompassing “thought, attention, memory, and will.” While it mentions chapters on topics including “Attention,” “Memory,” and “Will,” it does not state that these are what “psychological field” refers to.

The definition therefore adds multiple specific explanatory elements (distinctness from bodily/neurological events; the particular set of processes as the referent) that are not provided or supported in the supplied text.
